questions.question: Tailwind CSS is best described as:

options.text: A utility-first CSS framework (compose styles via small classes like p-4, flex)
A component library with prebuilt buttons

questions.explanation: Tailwind is utility-first: you build UIs by applying atomic classes (flex, p-4, text-sm) directly in markup.

questions.question: The JIT engine (Tailwind v3+) does:

options.text: Generates only the CSS for classes actually used in your markup
Loads all possible classes upfront (massive file)

questions.explanation: JIT scans content files and emits just the used utilities, keeping the bundle tiny and enabling arbitrary values (e.g. w-[330px]).

questions.question: Responsive variants use a prefix like:

options.text: md:flex, lg:grid (breakpoint prefix before the utility)

questions.explanation: Breakpoint prefixes (sm:, md:, lg:) apply utilities at min-width breakpoints — mobile-first.

questions.question: Customization (colors, spacing) is done in:
questions.explanation: tailwind.config.js defines content paths and theme.extend tokens; the engine reads it to generate utilities.

questions.question: A downside of utility classes is:

options.text: Markup can become verbose / harder to read for complex components

questions.explanation: Verbose class strings are the common critique; mitigated by @apply, components, and frameworks (Angular/React) extracting repeated patterns.

questions.question: To reuse a group of utilities as a component you can use:

options.text: @apply in CSS or extract a component class/template

questions.explanation: @apply composes utilities into a custom class; or build a component so the class list lives in one place.

questions.question: Arbitrary values are written as:
questions.explanation: JIT supports arbitrary values in brackets for one-off needs without editing the config.

questions.question: Tailwind differs from BEM in that:

options.text: Tailwind uses utility classes in markup; BEM uses semantic, single-class names in stylesheets

questions.explanation: Tailwind = utility classes in HTML; BEM = semantic naming in CSS. They address styling differently (composition vs naming).
